cases.prompt: We only find out something broke when a reader tells us. The only checks that drive the real site look at where the home page's links point, and at one address that shouldn't exist.
cases.rationale: The project really does ship one thin browser-driven spec, and its two tests are exactly the two the prompt describes — the home page's post links, and an unknown slug's status. The question is which journeys a suite that drives the whole system should cover, which is the end-to-end capability's subject. The three design skills are excluded because the prompt mentions a page and its links, and a skill that routes on those nouns rather than on what is being asked has misrouted.

cases.prompt: I'm about to commit this. Our log is already a mess and I'd rather not add to it.
cases.rationale: Bare, because the subject is a change in flight and a situated workspace structurally has none: materialization refuses to leave anything uncommitted, so every probe would open on a clean tree with nothing to write a message about. The commit-message capability owns the header contract, and the prompt carries the whole of what routes to it. The design trio is excluded because a message is not a surface.

cases.prompt: We'd like to pull in a library that only ships as an ES module. Will the test setup here cope with it?
cases.rationale: Want-shaped rather than symptom-shaped: nothing is broken, so a prompt claiming a failing suite would describe something the model cannot find. The runner is the subject — transform configuration is what decides the answer — and the runner this project uses is not the other one, which is what makes the exclusion a real boundary rather than a formality.

cases.prompt: The language tags on our posts are written two different ways — some carry a region and some don't — and nothing stops the next one being written in a third shape.
cases.rationale: The catalogue really does carry two spellings of one language — a tag with a region on every post, and one translation tagged with the bare subtag — while both fields are typed as plain strings, so the inconsistency is something the model can confirm by reading rather than a premise it has to accept. Constraining a string that must have a shape is the schema layer's subject, and the project already does exactly that for one other field. Security is excluded because authored content is not untrusted input: the schema capability hands that question to the security one by name, so reaching for it here means routing on the smell of validation rather than on whose data this is. The maintainability capability is permitted because two spellings of one value is legitimately its lens too.

cases.prompt: We want to accept a page number in the URL. It arrives as text, it might be missing, and it might be there but empty.
cases.rationale: The trap is a coercion that turns an empty string into zero rather than into a missing value, which is a schema question. The framework capability may fire because the value arrives through a route's own parameters, and that is a legitimate second half of the same answer.

cases.prompt: The bit of logic that decides which language a reader is shown has no tests at all. What should the tests actually be checking?
cases.rationale: One shared module genuinely ships without a spec while its neighbour has one, so the gap is the project's rather than planted. The question is what to assert, not which runner API expresses it — but situated in a project that has a runner, reaching for that runner's capability is defensible, so it moved from excluded to permitted. The other runner is still excluded: it is not the one here.

cases.prompt: I want to write down how we roll back a bad release. Where does that belong, and how much of it belongs there?
cases.rationale: The deployment notes already carry a two-line rollback paragraph that punts the harder case elsewhere, so the 'where does it belong' half opens on a real answer and the 'how much of it belongs there' half is the live question — which is the shape the prompt asks in. A runbook is a procedure a reader follows, not a statement of what the product is, so it belongs to the document-authoring capability rather than to the corpus that records product behaviour. The two are adjacent enough that a model reading only the word 'documentation' will pick the wrong one, which is the boundary being measured.

cases.prompt: Before I ask anyone to look at this, go through what I've changed and tell me what you'd raise.
cases.rationale: Bare, because the subject is a change in flight and a situated workspace structurally has none: materialization refuses to leave anything uncommitted, and no probe holds a shell, so there is no diff any amount of reading could reach. Reviewing an existing change is the review capability's whole subject; the change-loop capability is excluded because it drives a change from plan to merge, and firing it here means the model heard 'branch' and reached for process rather than for judgement.

cases.prompt: We want readers to be able to send us a correction on a post. What do we need to be careful about on the way in?
cases.rationale: A write path in this framework runs on the server with no gate of its own, and knowing that is the framework capability's subject. The mobile framework is excluded because this is a web project and selecting it means the model routed on 'app' without reading. Security and schema may both legitimately fire — the answer has an authorization half and a validation half.

cases.prompt: When we change a post the site keeps serving the old one until someone redeploys. We'd like it to pick the change up on its own.
cases.rationale: The posts really are a build-time module here, so 'stale until a redeploy' is what the project does rather than a defect claimed about it. Caching and revalidation on the server is the framework's question. The server-state library may fire — it answers the same-sounding question on the client — and whether that is right depends on reading which side renders this, so it is permitted rather than excluded.

cases.prompt: We want readers to be able to leave a note on a post, with a bit of formatting allowed.
cases.rationale: Formatted text from a stranger rendered into a page is the injection case, and output encoding is the security capability's subject. The schema capability is permitted rather than excluded because validating what arrives is a real part of the answer — it is simply not the part that stops the page executing it.

cases.prompt: The language-matching logic has grown a handful of helpers and I can't hold the whole thing in my head any more.
cases.rationale: There is a real module with several exported helpers and a documented resolution order to read. Cohesion and what belongs in one unit is the maintainability capability's subject. Review is excluded because nothing here is a change to judge — the request is to restructure, not to assess.

cases.prompt: I'm about to change the order we fall back through when a reader's language doesn't match. What else has to move with it?
cases.rationale: The fallback order is stated twice — in the module's own comments and in the project's agent instructions — so the answer is genuinely 'more than the code'. The deployment notes are the near miss: they name the module and then point at it for the order rather than restating it, so a model that moves them has misread which documents actually carry the claim. Keeping the documents that describe the product true as it changes is the living-specification capability's subject.

cases.prompt: I want to write up the reader-corrections idea properly before anyone builds it, so we can argue about it while it's still cheap.
cases.rationale: A boundary case with two right answers: one capability owns the document's sections and the phrasing of a requirement, the other owns the sentences inside whatever is being written. Both firing is the healthy outcome; the coverage line is what tells contention from a gap.

cases.prompt: Where should the requirements for something we haven't built yet live, as opposed to the description of how the thing already works?
cases.rationale: The two capabilities divide the same territory by tense: one owns the change about to be made, the other the steady state. The prompt names both halves without naming either capability, so a model that reads only 'documentation' will pick whichever it saw first.

cases.prompt: This is being called ready. Was it actually checked, or does it just look finished?
cases.rationale: Bare, for the same structural reason as the review case: the subject is a change being called ready, and a situated workspace is always a clean tree with nothing in flight to judge. Whether a change carries adequate verification evidence is its own question, distinct from whether the code is correct. Review may legitimately fire beside it — the two run together on a real pull request — so it is permitted rather than excluded.

cases.prompt: We want a link in an email to open the app straight onto one particular deck rather than the list.
cases.rationale: The app has a real parameterised route under its routes directory and a scheme declared in its config, so a link resolving to a screen is something the model can trace. The web framework is excluded: selecting it means routing on the word 'link' without reading what kind of project this is.

cases.prompt: The prompt asking for the camera doesn't say why we want it, and we'd like it to, in our own words.
cases.rationale: The case patch replaces the app's own permission copy with the boilerplate line a project gets when it never wrote one, so the symptom is real: the string the model finds genuinely says nothing about why the camera is wanted. That copy comes from a config plugin and reaches the native build through generation rather than through a hand-edited native file — which is the framework capability's subject and is exactly the thing a model that has not read the config gets wrong. The two component capabilities are excluded because nothing here is a component question.

cases.prompt: We've settled what goes on the screen for changing a card that already exists, and in what order. Now I need it to actually look like the rest of the app.
cases.rationale: Want-shaped, and the want is real: the app can add a card but has no screen for changing one, so there is nothing already carrying the treatment being asked for. Every screen that does exist draws from the theme, which is what 'the rest of the app' resolves to once the model looks. This is the hand-off point between the two design capabilities, stated from the side that has already passed it. The low-fidelity capability is excluded because its work is finished by the first sentence, and firing it means the model matched on 'what goes on the screen' rather than reading the second.

cases.prompt: One of the small controls flips between two looks by tacking an extra style on when a flag is set. It's already awkward and we now need a third look for it.
cases.rationale: The patch reverts one leaf control to the platform's own stylesheet and a conditional style array, and removes its focused state, so both halves are real in the workspace: two looks today, and a third genuinely wanted. The flag is derived inside the component rather than taken as a prop, which is why the prompt describes the conditional rather than the signature. The project's own instructions already say why this shape is wrong here. Both design capabilities are excluded: nothing is being designed, an existing look is being expressed differently.

cases.prompt: Every time the app restarts, our numbers treat the same person as somebody new.
cases.rationale: The patch moves the identity-clearing call out of the sign-out path and into startup, which is exactly the symptom. The fix is a property of one vendor's SDK — where its reset belongs and how its identity is persisted — so the vendor-neutral capability is the wrong reach, and this is the sharpest of the pairs that measure that boundary.

cases.prompt: Nothing walks a brand-new author from arriving to their first published post. I want to see the whole path before we build any of it.
cases.rationale: The product deliberately has no onboarding flow, so the request is to breadboard a path rather than to change one. The styling capability is excluded because there is nothing to style yet, and reaching for it means the model heard 'build' rather than 'before we build'.

cases.prompt: Authors have asked for a screen showing how their posts are doing. Nothing like it exists, and I don't want to talk about colour yet.
cases.rationale: The prompt states the boundary in the author's own words rather than in the capability's vocabulary, which is what changed from the version that said 'grey-box the regions'. Both excluded capabilities are the ones the second sentence rules out.

cases.prompt: The same handful of colours is typed out again in every place we style something, and when we want to change how the product looks we have to go hunting for all of them.
cases.rationale: One colour is written out in five separate stylesheets and two more in three and two, with nothing naming any of them, so the symptom is countable rather than a matter of taste. A deliberate two-answer case: what the palette should be belongs to one capability and where a shared value lives belongs to the other, and both name design tokens in their own discovery text. Both firing is the healthy outcome and the coverage line is what distinguishes contention from a gap.

cases.prompt: We want to keep a short summary next to each post, and it has to survive a restart.
cases.rationale: A negative case: the library ships no capability for schema migrations, so the right outcome is that none of the design capabilities fires on a prompt that mentions posts and a summary. It names no required skill on purpose — the finding here would be a spurious selection, not a miss.

cases.prompt: We'd like to be able to watch back what an author was doing when something breaks, without paying to capture everybody.
cases.rationale: Session replay and its sampling are one vendor's product with its own cost model, and this project wires that vendor. The neutral capability is excluded because sampling replay is not a vendor-agnostic idea; the error-tracking vendor is excluded because it is the other SDK in the same project, which is what makes this the sharper exclusion of the two.

cases.prompt: Before we add any more, I want a rule for how these names are formed — one that would still make sense if we swapped the tool out.
cases.rationale: The strict half of the same pair. The last clause is what moves it: a scheme that outlives the tool is a vendor-neutral question, so firing the vendor capability means the model routed on the SDK it found in the project rather than on what was asked.

cases.prompt: The errors coming back from the live site are unreadable — single letters where the function names should be.
cases.rationale: The patch breaks the source-map upload that the project ships working, so the symptom is real and its cause is readable in the build configuration. Which build step restores a name to a minified frame is the vendor capability's subject; the neutral capability may fire on the surrounding question of what an error report should carry.

cases.prompt: When the call out to the site's host fails and we try again, what level should that be recorded at? And the one after the last attempt?
cases.rationale: There is a real retrying call site with a levelled logger beside it. Which level a recoverable failure earns versus a final one is a vendor-neutral judgement; the error-tracking vendor is excluded because it is wired in this same project and reaching for it means routing on 'fails' rather than on 'what level'.

cases.prompt: Saving a draft leaves the title and timestamp on the post list stale until something else refetches it.
cases.rationale: The save path writes the record it just saved into the detail cache and never invalidates the site's post list, so the list keeps showing the old title — a gap the project has rather than one planted in it, and the publish mutation beside it does invalidate both. The framework capability is excluded because this project has no such framework, so selecting it means the model routed on the symptom's shape rather than on what it read.

cases.prompt: Switching from one customer's site to another shows the wrong site's posts for a moment before it corrects itself.
cases.rationale: The patch collides two cache keys that the project ships separated, and there is a committed test asserting they stay apart — so the defect is real and its fingerprint is readable. What identifies an entry in the cache is the server-state capability's subject; the component capability is excluded because nothing about the component is wrong.

cases.prompt: There are settings in our test configuration that don't seem to do anything any more.
cases.rationale: The patch adds options the current major silently ignores, which is the exact failure the runner capability exists to catch — silently ignored, so nothing fails and only knowing the option surface finds it. The other runner is excluded because it is not the one here; the browser-suite capability because the question is configuration, not scenarios.

cases.prompt: One of the tests that drives an actual browser passes on my machine and fails about a third of the time on the shared one.
cases.rationale: A deliberate two-answer case, and the patch makes the race real. One capability owns the runner's browser mode and its waiting primitives; the other owns the discipline of polling rather than sleeping. Both firing is the healthy outcome.

cases.prompt: Several screens each pull the same thing out of the address bar the same way, and each spells out its own waiting and failure branches. Where should that live?
cases.rationale: Three route components read the same parameter with the same empty-string default, and four spell out their own pending and error branches, so the repetition is countable rather than asserted. Extracting shared logic out of components is the component capability's subject. The styling capability is excluded because nothing about the appearance is in question.

cases.prompt: I need to update an issue's description from a script, but what the read gives me back doesn't match what's stored. How do I do this without wrecking it?
cases.rationale: Bare, because a materialized workspace has no issues, pull requests or labels — situating is what removes the substrate. Being bare, the prompt states its subject rather than only a symptom. Operating GitHub safely from a shared identity is the operation capability's subject; the review capability is excluded because nothing is being judged.

cases.prompt: I want to cut this SKILL.md's body down. How do I keep its description routing to it afterwards?
cases.rationale: Bare, because a mock project deliberately holds no SKILL.md files: holding them is what would turn discovery into instruction-following. Authoring owns what a description has to say; management owns where a skill's source lives and how it is installed, which is a different question.

cases.prompt: The installed copy of a skill no longer matches the source it was built from. What should I do about that?
cases.rationale: Bare for the same reason as the case above. This is the mirror of it: the two-tier storage model and the drift between a source and an installed copy belong to management, not to how the skill is written.

cases.prompt: I'm picking up a change in this project. What should I do before I start writing code?
cases.rationale: A wiring case rather than a discovery case. This project's own instructions describe a plan-first, reviewed-by-another process in its own words and name no skill, so the question is whether that generic language is enough for the change-loop capability to surface. The mandated population is reported separately for exactly this reason: a real consumer names this capability outright, so a shortfall here is a statement about wiring rather than about the description.

cases.prompt: I've just cloned this. What do I have to run and pass before I put a change up?
cases.rationale: A wiring case. The previous version of this prompt claimed the commands were not written down anywhere, which situating makes false — all three mocks document them. Rewritten as an honest question, it asks whether the baseline development capability surfaces when someone needs to find out how a project is actually run.

cases.prompt: Which major version of the framework is this on, and what changed in the one before it that we'd care about?
cases.rationale: A wiring case, and the one whose recorded result this rebuild re-reads rather than re-runs. Half the question is answerable by reading the project and half is not, so the right behaviour is to look one up rather than recall it. The framework capability may legitimately fire on the first half.
